newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's sokaiya a mixture of thugs and accountants.
newsitem.headline: Japan's sokaiya a mixture of thugs and accountants.

text.p: The infamous "sokaiya" racketeers at the heart of a payoff scandal gripping Tokyo's financial world are a uniquely Japanese mixture of thugs and high-powered accountants.
Their methods range from crude threats of violence to sophisticated probing of financial missteps by company management which they threaten to question at annual shareholders' meetings.
The word sokaiya roughly translates as someone who is in the business of shareholder meetings.

They describe themselves as activists standing up for shareholders who are ignored by Japanese corporations bound together by the age-old practice of cross-shareholding. Sokaiya often claim to know more about a target company's financial state than its own senior executives.
One group even has its own Internet home page and a senior figure in the sokaiya world boasts of his degree from the prestigious Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

Their targets are often companies that have something to fear from disclosure of details about their condition, especially those with long-entrenched management structures which are not open to scrutiny by shareholders.
After a number of scandals in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Japan banned corporations from making payoffs to racketeers in 1983.
But the racketeers have proved more inventive than the law. Since straight payoffs were made illegal they have engaged in a variety of methods to extract cash.

One popular ploy is to publish slim newsletters or magazines, sometimes containing a few pages of poetry, and charge company libraries thousands of dollars to subscribe. Nomura Securities, at the heart of the latest scandal, recently said it was dropping 700 such subscriptions,
They also arrange corporate "seminars" with high attendance fees.
But their methods are not always so subtle. They have been known to use old-fashioned threats of violence and police blame sokaiya for the 1994 murder of an executive of Fuji Photo Film Co.
Their numbers have declined sharply from the nearly 5,000 believed active before their activities were outlawed.
But experts say that 500 to 600 major companies still have ties to the racketeers.
"Unless they arrest all of their top executives along with the sokaiya, things probably won't really change that much," said Tokuo Sakaguchi, a lawyer and shareholder activist.
